title: Properties of the retained localization
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $T\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}R$ a Zariski closed subset, and $R_{[T]}$ the retained localization [def-weil-pbc-retained-localization]. The map $R\to R_{[T]}$ is ind-Zariski [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra]. Its points are precisely the pairs $(x,y)$ of primes of $R$ with $x\in T$ and $y\subseteq x$, and the canonical map from $R_y$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] to the local ring at $(x,y)$ is an isomorphism. If every point of $T$ is closed in $\operatorname{Spec}R$, then $\operatorname{Spec}R_{[T]}$ is w-local [def-weil-pbc-w-local], with closed point set identified with $T$ (with its patch topology). If, under this closed-point hypothesis, $T=V(J)$ for an ideal $J\subseteq R$, then the canonical quotient map $R/J\to R_{[T]}/JR_{[T]}$ is an isomorphism.

proof.text: Put $C=R^w$ and $B=R_{[T]}$. The definition [def-weil-pbc-w-localization] makes $R\to C$ ind-Zariski. Each $C\to C_{e_E}$ is a principal localization, hence an ind-Zariski building block [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra]. Composition and filtered-colimit stability [lem-weil-pbc-ind-etale-stability], applied to the reverse-inclusion diagram in [def-weil-pbc-retained-localization], give $R\to B$ ind-Zariski. The index is a set of subsets of Spec R and is filtered by finite intersection; it need not be a sequence.

For an idempotent $e$, inverting $e$ is the same as imposing $e=1$, since $e(1-e)=0$. Consequently $B=C/K$, where $K$ is the ideal generated by all $1-e_E$ with $E\supseteq T$; both rings have the same universal property for ring maps from $C$. Its primes are exactly the primes of $C$ containing $K$, with the subspace topology: the inverse image of $D(\bar c)$ is $D(c)\cap V(K)$. At such a prime $p$, each $e_E$ is a unit and hence is 1 in $C_p$, so $K C_p=0$ and the canonical map $C_p\to B_{p/K}$ sends $c/s$ to $(c+K)/(s+K)$. Its inverse sends $(c+K)/(s+K)$ to $c/s$: changing a lift by an element of $K$ changes the fraction by zero because $K C_p=0$. These maps are inverse by the defining equality relation on fractions [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime].

source.place: Proof, first paragraph: expand filtered idempotent localizations

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-w-localization-points], a point of Spec C is a pair $(x,y)$ with $y\subseteq x$, with canonical local ring $R_y$. By the selector definition [def-weil-pbc-retained-localization], $e_E$ is 1 exactly on pairs whose first coordinate is in $E$. Thus step 2 retains precisely those pairs with $x\in\bigcap_{E\supseteq T}E$. This intersection is $T$: write $T=V(I)$; if $x\notin T$, choose $f\in I\setminus x$, and the constructible neighbourhood $V(f)$ contains $T$ and omits $x$. This proves the point and canonical local-ring assertions without invoking an uncited inverse-limit theorem.

source.place: Proof, first paragraph: intersection of constructible neighbourhoods and listed pairs

proof.text: The map to the patch space of first coordinates has clopen inverse images of constructible subsets, furnished by the selector idempotents. The fibres are the components Spec $R_x$ of [lem-weil-pbc-w-localization-points]. The retained subspace is a union of these entire fibres. Each fibre stays connected, and any connected subset of the retained subspace is connected in Spec C, hence lies in one ambient fibre; its components are therefore exactly these fibres for $x\in T$. Within the retained fibre $\operatorname{Spec}R_x$, the closure of $(x,y)$ contains $(x,x)$ because $yR_x\subseteq xR_x$, so its closure in the retained spectrum also contains $(x,x)$; if $y\ne x$, this is a different retained point. Conversely $(x,x)$ was already closed in $\operatorname{Spec}C$, hence remains closed in the retained subspace. Thus the globally closed points are exactly the diagonal points, one per component. The diagonal point set is the intersection with the closed diagonal point set of Spec C, so is closed, with induced topology the patch topology on $T$. This is w-locality by [def-weil-pbc-w-local], in particular under the stated hypothesis that points of $T$ are closed in Spec R.

source.place: Proof, first paragraph: components and closed diagonal points

proof.text: Now assume $T=V(J)$ and every point of $T$ is closed. Put $A=R/J$ and $D=B/JB$. Primes of a quotient are the primes containing its defining ideal, by inverse image and quotient of ideals. Thus points of Spec D are pairs with $J\subseteq y\subseteq x$ and $x\in T$. Since every prime containing $J$ is maximal, $y=x$. The induced continuous map Spec D $\to$ Spec A [def-weil-affine-spectrum] is consequently a bijection, taking $(x,x)$ to $x/J$. All primes of A and D are maximal.

source.place: Proof, second paragraph: prime calculation for the quotient

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-zero-dimensional-spectrum-profinite] separately to A and D. Their spectra are compact Hausdorff; hence the continuous bijection of step 5 is a homeomorphism by [lem-weil-pbc-compact-hausdorff-bijection].

source.place: Proof, second paragraph: compact Hausdorff quotient spectra

proof.text: At the point $(x,x)$, step 3 identified $B_p$ canonically with $R_x$. Quotienting and localizing commute here by the explicit fraction maps $(a+J)/s\mapsto a/s+JR_x$ and their inverses [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]: in the inverse direction $a/s+JR_x$ goes to $(a+J)/(s+J)$; if a difference lies in $JR_x$, multiplying by a common denominator outside $x$ makes its numerator lie in $J$, which is exactly equality of the quotient fractions. Thus the local rings of A at $x/J$ and of D at the point over it are both $R_x/JR_x$, and the map induced by $A\to D$ is the identity on these fractions. The homeomorphism from step 6 and [lem-weil-pbc-affine-homeomorphism-local-rings] imply the canonical ring map $R/J\to B/JB$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Proof, second paragraph: canonical quotient local rings and ring isomorphism

proof_origin.place: Proof, both paragraphs, with the omitted fraction and topological arguments expanded
